channel: Super is the main way an AI share-market fall reaches Australian households. About half of large funds’ investments are overseas, with roughly 31% in listed international shares, much of it in US markets where AI stocks dominate. Funds also hold growing unlisted assets, whose values are updated more slowly.
reading: Balances hit a record of nearly A$4.8tn in 2025–26 and rose 5.2% in the June quarter as markets recovered. The RBA calls super a source of stability but wants funds to strengthen how they manage sudden cash calls, for example from currency hedges when the dollar falls or from members switching or withdrawing.
watch: APRA’s September-quarter statistics (December), and how funds handle currency-hedge cash calls if the Australian dollar drops sharply.
source: Financial Standard 1 Sep 2026; ABS Financial Accounts (24 Sep 2026); Super Members Council/ASFA paper on super and international investments (Sep 2025 data); RBA Financial Stability Review Oct 2026

channel: Two forces pull in opposite directions. The AI boom itself has added to inflation through global energy and equipment demand, and the RBA cites it directly. A bust would cool demand, but a falling Australian dollar, which tends to drop when global markets sell off, makes imports and fuel dearer.
reading: Headline inflation was 4.3% in the year to September (trimmed mean 3.6%), driven by fuel (+23.6%) and electricity (+12.8%). The RBA raised the cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November, an 18-year high, in a 6–3 split vote. Stronger-than-expected wages on 18 November left markets pricing about a 27% chance of another hike by February. The Australian dollar was near US$0.67 on 18 November.
watch: October CPI on 25 November, and whether the RBA holds in December as Westpac expects.
asof: CPI Sep 2026; cash rate 3 Nov; market pricing 18 Nov
source: ABS CPI September 2026 (28 Oct); RBA decision 3 Nov 2026 via Westpac IQ and ABC; ABC News business live 18 Nov (Bloomberg swaps, AUD)

factor: Government investment in the AI economy
channel: Government spending on AI itself is modest. The bigger exposure is policy that relies on private money: the National AI Plan (December 2025) aims to attract data-centre investment, and states compete for projects. If global AI investors pull back, promised data centres, jobs and grid upgrades could stall.
reading: Direct commitments are small, such as A$29.9m for an AI Safety Institute. On 18 November Nvidia said it expects to develop up to 2 gigawatts of data-centre land, power and shell capacity in Australia by the end of 2027 with partners including Firmus and Sharon.ai, more than the ~1.6 GW the industry says exists today. That deepens the link to the US AI cycle. AEMO reports more than 40% of data-centre projects proposed since 2025 have dropped out or gone backwards in the grid queue. The RBA’s forecasts assume no AI productivity boost and no regional data-centre hub.
watch: Whether Nvidia’s Australian plans get firm financing and grid connections, data-centre cancellations in Sydney and Melbourne, and any change to the National AI Plan.
source: CommBank on the National AI Plan (2 Dec 2025); AEMO 2026 ESOO via Data Centre Magazine; RBA Statement on Monetary Policy Nov 2026 via Westpac IQ; ABC News business live 18 Nov

channel: Energy, food and finance are the systems people need to keep working in a downturn. Energy is tied to AI through data-centre power demand; food through fuel and fertiliser costs; finance through banks, super and private credit.
reading: Energy: data centres use about 5 TWh a year (~3% of the main grid), forecast to reach ~34 TWh (~13%) by 2035–36; electricity prices are up 12.8% in a year and fuel 23.6%. Food: food prices are up 3.2%. Finance: the RBA says banks hold large capital buffers and could keep lending through a severe shock; private credit is about 10% of business debt and more exposed to property than to AI.
watch: Electricity prices and grid reliability over summer, fuel prices while the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, any stress in property-focused private credit funds, and APRA’s planned 2027 stress test of how AI-driven economic change could affect financial stability (announced 12 Nov).
source: AEMO 2026 ESOO via Data Centre Magazine; ABS CPI September 2026; RBA Financial Stability Review Oct 2026; APRA via MLex 13 Nov 2026

channel: An AI bust would reach jobs mainly through confidence and spending: falling super and share balances make households spend less (RBA analysis finds a 20% fall in AI shares would noticeably cut household spending), and stalled data-centre and tech projects cut construction and tech hiring.
reading: Unemployment rose to 4.9% in October, the highest since October 2021, as 43,500 jobs were lost (mostly part-time) and participation fell to 66.6%. Youth unemployment reached 11.3%, and Victoria and Tasmania are highest at 5.4%. Underemployment eased slightly to 6.2%. The rate is already close to the 5.1% the RBA expected only by the end of 2028.
watch: November jobs figures on 17 December, and whether rising unemployment shifts the RBA away from further hikes.
source: ABS Labour Force October 2026 (19 Nov); NewsCop 19 Nov; RBA Statement on Monetary Policy Nov 2026 via Westpac IQ; RBA research reported by InvestingLive

channel: Whether pay keeps up with prices decides how much buffer households have going into a downturn. Falling real wages plus 18-year-high mortgage rates leave less room to absorb job losses or a hit to super.
reading: Wages rose 1.1% in the September quarter, the fastest in nearly three years, and 3.5% over the year (private 3.4%, public 3.9%), helped by the 4.75% award wage rise. Prices rose 4.3% in the year to September, so real wages have now gone backwards for a full year, though the gap has narrowed to under a percentage point.
watch: October CPI on 25 November, and whether stronger wages keep the RBA leaning towards another hike.
source: ABS Wage Price Index September 2026 (18 Nov); ABC News business live 18 Nov; ABS CPI September 2026 (28 Oct)
